To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a team of MAVs can use a combination of a hierarchical decomposition of an environment, random finite sets, and mutual information to estimate the number of and locations of targets in an unknown environment, even when targets are unknown and the sensors are unreliable.
a team of MAVs can be used to discover the location and number of buried targets in a field, even in the presence of uncertainty, by following a gradient of mutual information.
a team of micro aerial vehicles can cooperatively detect and localize multiple permanent magnet anomalies in a cluttered, unknown environment.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. (1) What are the fundamental challenges in using multiple MAVs to detect magnetic anomalies in an unknown environment? (2) How should the robots coordinate their sensing and exploration activities to achieve their goal?
the problem of active magnetic anomaly detection using multiple micro aerial vehicles.
the development of algorithms that enable multiple robots to cooperatively explore an unknown environment to discover and estimate the locations of magnetic targets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed method is capable of detecting and localizing an arbitrary number of targets in an unknown environment, and that this can be accomplished with a small team of micro aerial vehicles, even in the face of sensor and communication failures, and with only a priori knowledge of the environment.

the proposed algorithm is capable of detecting and locating an arbitrary number of permanent magnets in an environment using only the measurements from a team of quad-rotor MAVs, with the ability to adapt to the number of targets in the scene.

the proposed approach is a novel and effective solution to the MAD problem, with the following contributions: 1) the first use of a hierarchical decomposition of an environment for a multi-robot MAD problem, 2) the first use and analysis of random finite sets in a multi-robot, multi-target estimation problem, and 3) the first use, to the best of our knowledge, of a mutual information gradient-based algorithm for a multi- robot, multi-target estimation and control problem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a framework for using a team of micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) to perform magnetic anomaly detection (MADS) and demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach on a team of quad-rotor MAVs.
we have successfully demonstrated the use of a team of MAVs for active MAD.
we have developed a framework that can be used for the estimation, control and planning of a team of robots to solve the magnetic anomaly detection problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the robots are able to autonomously and quickly localize a number of targets, even in the presence of false positive and false negatives.
a team of small, cheap robots with simple sensors can perform a complex, information theoretic task.
a small team of robots can cooperatively estimate the number and locations of targets in an environment, even when the robots do not know the targets exist.
